trying.q: We offer this book as a gift, addict to addict, and hope our love and concern for every addict who is trying our way of life comes across as strongly as we feel it.

turn.q: It doesn’t matter where we come from or how good or bad we think we’ve had it; when we finally turn to Narcotics Anonymous and the Twelve Steps, we begin to find relief.

turned.q: Throughout the process of the Fifth Step, we turned to that Power when we were fearful, and we received the courage we needed to complete the step.

turning.q: Turning our will and our lives over to the care of our Higher Power provides a solution to the problems created by a life based in self-will, resentment, and control.

turns.q: Our hope turns to faith as our lives begin to improve.

twelfth.q: We believe that the steps are presented in a manner that encompasses the diversity of our fellowship and is reflective of the spiritual awakening described in our Twelfth Step.

twelve.q: The book you have in your hands is a discussion of the Twelve Steps and Twelve Traditions of Narcotics Anonymous.

two.q: We saw only two choices: either keep fighting to control our using or just cave in completely and let our lives fall to pieces.

tying.q: Lending our name to a related facility or outside enterprise—allowing an addiction treatment facility, for example, to call itself The NA Medical Center—is the ultimate endorsement, permanently tying our primary purpose to theirs in the public eye.

type.q: Most of us don’t have much experience with the type of self-appraisal we are about to do, and we must have the guidance and support of our sponsor in order to understand what we’re doing.

types.q: We are now looking for the people, places, and institutions we harmed, not just the types of harm we inflicted.

ultimate.q: The experience shared by others is just that: experience , not ultimate answers to the mysteries of life.

unable.q: When we are having trouble in a particular area of our lives or when we feel unable to stay clean, our Higher Power can help; we only need to ask.

unattractive.q: We may think that if no one knows about them, our more unattractive characteristics will go away.

unbearable.q: The resulting pain might well be unbearable.

uncertain.q: Some of us have a remarkable talent for telling the truth, in no uncertain terms, to an addict literally dying to hear it.

uncertainty.q: When we first look at making the decision called for in this step, we are likely to have questions, uncertainty, and even fear about what we are being asked to do.

uncomfortable.q: We make a list of our resentments, for they often play a large part in making our recovery uncomfortable.

unconditional.q: Although this may feel like unconditional willingness, many of us have discovered that our willingness grew as we learned to trust a Power greater than ourselves.

unconscious.q: …lief that we can use again after a certain amount of time clean; a conscious or unconscious decision to work only certain steps. With the help of other recovering addicts, we can find ways to put our reservation…

uncover.q: We begin to uncover the pure and loving spirit that lies at the core of our being as we look for our character assets.

undergoing.q: We trust that we are undergoing a fundamental transformation, even though we may not yet understand its full implication for our lives.

underlying.q: We finally see that all the devices we use to keep other people away are unnecessary at best and, more often than not, are the underlying cause of the pain we suffer in our relationships.

understand.q: Through working the First Step we will address the obsession, the compulsion, the denial, and what many have termed a “spiritual void.” As we examine and acknowledge all these aspects of our disease, we start to understand our powerlessness.

understanding.q: We hope you will find personal growth, understanding, and empathy in the following pages.

understood.q: …We made a decision to turn our will and our lives over to the care of God as we understood Him .” The surrender we experience in Step One, coupled with the hope and belief we find in Step Two, make us ready and…

undertake.q: The search for a God of our own understanding is one of the most important efforts we will undertake in our recovery.

unfaithful.q: If we believed in monogamy but were unfaithful to our partners, what did we do so that we could live with our compromised principles?

unhappiness.q: For instance, at some time in our lives, we may feel unhappy but not know exactly what is causing such unhappiness.

unique.q: Our self-obsession blinded us to this, making us feel unique.

united.q: The fellowship grows and our common welfare increases as a result of our united efforts.

universal.q: Though each individual’s experience of a spiritual awakening varies, some experiences are so common as to be almost universal.

unlike.q: Unlike the admission we made in the First Step, which was made in desperation, the admission we made in Step Five was voluntary.

unlimited.q: Just as our freedom to have a God of our own understanding is unlimited, so is our freedom to communicate with our Higher Power in whatever ways work for us.

unmanageable.q: Step One 3 STEP ONE “We admitted that we were powerless over our addiction, that our lives had become unmanageable.” As addicts, we have each experienced the pain, loneliness, and despair of addiction.

unnatural.q: When we first begin to practice these principles, they may seem very unnatural to us.

unreasonable.q: We can stop making unreasonable demands on others and begin to give of ourselves in relationships.

upholding.q: Through upholding the principles of recovery, we seek a life of harmony and peace.

urge.q: We may feel an urge to fall back on what seems easier: the familiar ways of our addiction.

use.q: Please use and enjoy this book.

used.q: All the lies, all the pretenses, all the rationalizations we had used to justify where we stood as a result of our drug use stopped working.

usefulness.q: Searching those options out and exploring their usefulness to us can be uncomfortable and time-consuming.

using.q: We may even have vowed to stop using altogether at a certain point.

usually.q: We usually had good intentions, but our day-to-day existence rarely measured up to those intentions.

valuable.q: We pray you will be moved to a new level of insight into your recovery and the valuable place you occupy as a member of Narcotics Anonymous.

value.q: We pray that this book truly represents the therapeutic value of one addict helping another.

values.q: We list the people, places, social values, institutions, and situations against which we bear anger.

varied.q: The ways in which we carry the message are as varied as our members.

variety.q: 10 It Works The disease of addiction can manifest itself in a variety of mental obsessions and compulsive actions that have nothing to do with drugs.

various.q: We come from various walks of life and experience, so it is natural that we bring with us differing concepts of spirituality.

vary.q: Again, our experiences are individual and vary widely from addict to addict.

vast.q: As we work Step Six, bridging the vast gulf that lies between fear and courage requires a great deal of willingness and trust on our part.

victim.q: Our idea that we have been a victim must go.

victims.q: We may have been victims of incest or rape.

view.q: As recovery becomes more central in our lives and we internalize the principles embodied in the steps, our view of the world changes profoundly.

viewed.q: We viewed the world around us as a hostile environment.

views.q: We forcefully share our views at the meeting.

vigorous.q: Groups demonstrate this when they offer vigorous, conscious support for addicts seeking to work the NA program.

vision.q: 38 It Works integrity to respect our confidences, and enough insight to help us keep the exact nature of our wrongs within our field of vision.

vital.q: The need for our own sense of spirituality is too vital to our recovery for us to neglect this highly personal process.

vitality.q: When we work to ensure the vitality of NA, we’re not working just for ourselves but for those yet to join us.

voice.q: We need to stay in tune with the voice of our conscience and listen to what it’s telling us.

void.q: Through working the First Step we will address the obsession, the compulsion, the denial, and what many have termed a “spiritual void.” As we examine and acknowledge all these aspects of our disease, we start to understand our powerlessness.

voluntary.q: Unlike the admission we made in the First Step, which was made in desperation, the admission we made in Step Five was voluntary.

volunteer.q: 138 It Works time or expertise for our members to fulfill on a strictly volunteer basis.

vote.q: Based upon the understanding gained by sharing group conscience, a group may move on to a vote in order to make decisions.

vulnerable.q: We’ll see the same difficulties with trust, refusal to be vulnerable, and perhaps a lifelong pattern of inability to make commitments.

walk.q: If we trust that there is growth despite the pain, we can walk through these difficult periods more readily.

walked.q: We walked into our first meeting with a spiritual void.

walking.q: We can cease questioning why painful things happen and trust that walking through the difficult times in our lives can strengthen our recovery.

walks.q: We come from various walks of life and experience, so it is natural that we bring with us differing concepts of spirituality.

want.q: Each one of us can believe in anything in which we want to believe.

wanted.q: We were always on the lookout for ways we could force things to go as we wanted.

wants.q: We can see only our immediate wants and needs.

warm.q: Some of us are especially warm and compassionate, able to reach an addict who has rarely been the recipient of kindness.

warning.q: Despite the warning signs that our drug use was out of control, we continued trying to justify it.

way.q: Each member of NA has contributed to this book in some way.

ways.q: However, the disease seems to affect us in the following general ways.

week.q: In attending to the details of their week in, week out routines, autonomous NA groups may lose sight of the bigger picture.

welcomed.q: Coming to NA has been described by many members as “coming home.” We find ourselves welcomed and accepted by other recovering addicts.

welfare.q: We may have drained community resources, exhibited offensive behavior in public, or refused to contribute to the general welfare.

well.q: The Third Step is our commitment to our own emotional, physical, and spiritual well-being.

went.q: Some of us went through the motions of life but allowed nothing to touch us emotionally.

whatever.q: Whatever our individual circumstances, our lives have been governed by obsessive, compulsive, self-seeking behavior, and the end result has been unmanageability.

whenever.q: We beat a hasty retreat whenever life caught up with us.

wherever.q: 60 It Works 60 STEP NINE “We made direct amends to such people wherever possible, except when to do so would injure them or others.” Now that we are willing to make amends to all the people w…

whether.q: We realize that, whether written or verbal, no discussion of something as personal and individual as recovery can be all things to all people.

white.q: Our White Booklet states, “There is one thing more than anything else that will defeat us in our recovery; this is an attitude of indifference or intolerance toward spiritual principles.

whole.q: Much of our problem seems to center in our search for something to make us feel whole.

wide.q: We do, however, need to surrender our reservations, excuses, rationalizations, and self-deceptions and go forward into recovery with our eyes wide open.

widely.q: Again, our experiences are individual and vary widely from addict to addict.

willing.q: Am I willing to do whatever it takes to recover?

willpower.q: It is quite likely that, before coming to NA, we never believed in any power but our own willpower, and that had failed us.

wisdom.q: The reasons our program works, the how and why of recovery, are found in many places: in each other, in our relationship with a Higher Power, in our hearts and minds, and finally, in the collective wisdom of our members.

wishes.q: Humility prepares us to set aside our personal wishes so that we can effectively serve our fellowship.

withdrew.q: Some of us withdrew physically and had little, if any, contact with anyone.

women.q: We cannot predict a higher success rate for addicts of a certain age, or those who used for a certain number of years, or women over men, or any other external factor.

wonder.q: Even though we are admitting our addiction, we may still wonder if this program will really work.

wonderful.q: Wonderful events are mixed with painful ones.

wondering.q: We find ourselves wondering how our amends will be received.

word.q: This book is not meant to be an exhaustive study of NA’s steps and traditions, nor is it meant to be the final word on any aspect of recovery or NA unity.

wording.q: The wording of the Third Tradition reflects the broad focus of our First Step.

words.q: The idea that these words applied to us may have made us cringe.

work.q: Learning to be honest is an ongoing process; we are able to become progressively more honest as we work the steps and continue to stay clean.

worked.q: We allow others to share what has worked for them.

worker.q: Humility is always a desirable state, whether we are asking the God of our understanding to remove our shortcomings, conducting business with a co-worker, or talking to a friend.

workers.q: Our romantic relationships, our friendships, and our interactions with family members, co-workers, and casual acquaintances are undergoing an astounding change.

working.q: Through working the First Step we will address the obsession, the compulsion, the denial, and what many have termed a “spiritual void.” As we examine and acknowledge all these aspects of our disease, we start to understand our powerlessness.

works.q: After all was said and done, one fundamental truth emerged as the crux of our program: IT WORKS .

world.q: We viewed the world around us as a hostile environment.

worldwide.q: The importance of our unity encourages our groups to look beyond their own little worlds to the common needs of the worldwide NA Fellowship, placing the welfare of the whole before their own.

worry.q: Step Three doesn’t free us from having to take action, but it does liberate us from excessive worry about the results.

worse.q: As long as we are using drugs, our lives will steadily get worse.

worth.q: Our self-esteem increases as we realize that what we have to share is worth such close attention.

wounded.q: All of a sudden, we’ll notice a wounded look in the eyes of a friend after we’ve acted on one of our less endearing traits.

wounds.q: As the pain of old wounds begins to fade, we begin to live more fully in the present.

wreckage.q: We justified our actions, despite the wreckage around us resulting from our addiction.

write.q: Some of us may want to write our inventory all at once; others spend some time writing each day.

writing.q: Though the process of writing a book about the experience of a fellowship as diverse as ours has been lengthy, we saw all the barriers and stumbling blocks fade away in the light of our primary purpose: to carry the message to the still-suffering addict.

written.q: We realize that, whether written or verbal, no discussion of something as personal and individual as recovery can be all things to all people.

wrong.q: We see it in all the things that are wrong with our lives.

wrongdoing.q: Step Eight 55 probably entail being absolved of any wrongdoing.

wrongs.q: The Fourth Step allows us to identify the patterns, behaviors, and beliefs that show us the exact nature of our wrongs.

wrote.q: The same honesty and courage we called upon as we wrote our inventory and shared it are just as vital in making our amends list.

yearning.q: The desire to stop using may not be clearly realized; it may be no more than a subtle yearning for relief from pain.

years.q: Many of us came to NA after spending years practicing dishonesty.

yes.q: We cannot simply say, “Yes, I’m ready.
